nameStory: Staurastrum aculeatum gets its name from the Greek words 'stauros' meaning cross and 'astron' meaning star, describing its distinctive star-like shape when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'aculeatum' comes from Latin meaning 'spiny' or 'prickly,' referring to the sharp projections that extend from its cell walls like tiny thorns.
description: Staurastrum aculeatum is a microscopic single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes. This tiny organism is shaped like a flattened star with spiny projections, typically measuring only about 30-50 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair). It belongs to a group called desmids, which are known for their beautiful geometric shapes and bright green color. You'll need a microscope to see these intricate living jewels, as they're completely invisible to the naked eye.

idTips.description: A slight pinching or groove runs across the middle of the cell, dividing it into two symmetrical halves

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Extremely small, requiring at least 100x magnification to see clearly - about the size of a large bacterium

habitat: This rare microscopic alga is found in clean, acidic freshwater environments like bog pools, pristine mountain ponds, and the shallow margins of undisturbed lakes throughout New England. It prefers nutrient-poor waters with soft, peaty substrates and is often associated with sphagnum moss communities. Look for it in remote locations away from agricultural runoff or urban development.

seasonality.spring: Peak growing season as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. Cells are most active and may be found reproducing by splitting in half.
seasonality.summer: Still present but may be less abundant in very warm water. Best viewing conditions in cooler, shaded pond areas during early morning hours.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may increase again as temperatures cool and autumn rains refresh water levels in small pools and bog environments.
seasonality.winter: Survives under ice in a dormant state, though active cells may still be found in slightly warmer spring-fed areas.

funFact: Despite being a single cell smaller than a pinhead, Staurastrum aculeatum is essentially a living crystal - it can only reproduce by splitting perfectly in half, creating two identical mirror-image copies of its intricate geometric shape, like a microscopic 3D printer making exact duplicates of itself.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other spiny desmids like Micrasterias or other Staurastrum species. The key is counting the number of arms in the star pattern and noting the specific arrangement of spines - aculeatum has a more regular, symmetrical spine pattern compared to its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: This species is considered an indicator of pristine water quality - finding it suggests you've discovered a truly unpolluted aquatic environment. The extreme rarity in New England (only one recorded observation) makes any sighting scientifically valuable and worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Staurastrum aculeatum differs from its many relatives by having more regularly arranged spines and a more symmetrical star shape compared to species like S. hystrix (which has longer, more chaotic spines) or S. orbiculare (which is more circular). The spine length and pattern are key - aculeatum's spines are moderate in length and evenly distributed, creating a balanced, almost snowflake-like appearance.
